## Compared with

Surveyed 2026-11-05 per `SURVEY-PLAYBOOK.md` (the D0 survey: every eager method of the two engines' DataFrame and Series index pages gets a verdict; their documentation read, no source). Stars and releases as recorded by `tabular`'s survey of 2026-11-02, from the GitHub API that day.

| Project | Language | Licence | Stars | Last release / push | What a user notices against this module |
|---|---|---|--:|---|---|
| [pandas-dev/pandas](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas) — **reference** | Python, C | BSD-3-Clause | 50.3k | v3.1.0 (2026-10-22) | The vocabulary and the NaN semantics most users know, the index (refused here, § What it is not), `read_csv`, the `dt` and `str` accessors, window functions, `describe`. |
| [pola-rs/polars](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars) — **fastest** (one thread, to measure) | Rust | MIT | 40.2k | py-2.1.0 (2026-10-25) | Expressions, the lazy optimizer, threads; null is not NaN. The same table model as this module: no index, a row is its position. |

**Where we are ahead:** exact i128 `sum_exact` and fx-convert-before-sum in `aggregate` (neither engine has them built in *(inferred)*); in `mutate` and the `window` integer operations an integer overflow is null, never a wrapped number (`aggregate` and `pivot` `sum` of an int column go through f64 and lose exactness past 2^53; `sum_exact` does not). **Where we are behind:** see Scope and § Backlog; speed: polars is faster on 9 of the 33 bench rows by more than 1.25× (§ Maturity).

## What this module is, and what it is not

`Frame` is a table as one typed array per column with a validity bitmap; every verb is
`(allocator, Frame, Spec) -> Frame`. It replaces `dataset` + `tabular` (the dataframe split
plan of 2026-11-05): the storage came from `dataset.Frame`, the verbs
from `tabular.frame`, and both stay in place until step R retires them.

**Not here, refused:** a row index or MultiIndex (pandas' index family, survey row 3: every
verb would carry its cost, and polars users do without — owner's decision 2026-11-05); a
lazy optimizer or SQL (row 78); chunked storage (79); Python-language mechanics (rows 6, 9,
14, 17, 22, 57); plotting and styling (72); Period dtype (70); Excel/SQL/pickle and other
client libraries (76). Arrow, Parquet and the other columnar formats (75) are separate
planned modules, `arrow` and `parquet`; so are pandas' other file formats (Feather, ORC, Iceberg,
HDF5, Stata, SAS, SPSS, `read_html`), and XML (`read_xml`/`to_xml`: an adapter over the sibling
`xml` module, so that this module's closure — consumed by applications — does not grow by a parser
it does not otherwise need; owner's decision 2026-11-10). Also refused (survey rows 103/108,
2026-11-10): polars' `Expr.ext`/`register_extension_type` and the global string cache (types
registered from Python; a categorical here carries its own dictionary); `pl.sql`/`sql_expr` and
`read_sql`/`to_sql` (a SQL engine, a database driver); `map_batches`, `pipe_with_dtype`, the
`from_*`/`to_dict`/`to_records`/`to_numpy` conversions, pickle and the clipboard (Python, NumPy or
Arrow objects: `FrameBuilder`, the callback verbs and `writeJson` are the equivalents here);
`defer`/`collect_all`/`explain_all` (the lazy engine); `approx_n_unique`/`approx_quantile` (the
exact `n_unique`/`quantile` answer them); `cumulative_eval` (marked unstable by polars; an
expanding `rollingMap` callback computes it); `cast_time_unit` (one unit, microseconds, for every
instant and duration, as PostgreSQL and DuckDB `TIMESTAMP`: there is no unit to change);
`set_sorted` (a hint to polars' optimizer; no verb here keeps or trusts a sortedness flag, the
sorted-input verbs check their input instead); `json_normalize` (`readJson` builds the nested
`struct`/`list` columns and `unnest` flattens them; the `sep`-joined key paths and `record_path`
projection of deep documents are `jsonshape`'s column key paths).

**Not here, by plan:** row verbs and `viaRows` (rule 3 of the plan: `Frame` is the only
table model, so the card measures the one path that exists); `dataset`'s private wire
(no rival, no public purpose).

## Design & invariants

**Storage follows the cells, not the declared `ColumnType`.** All cells of one `Value` tag
(or null) get that tag's array; a mix gets `.boxed`, a plain `[]Value`. A null cell holds 0
in its array and has its bit clear; NaN is a value in storage, but every verb counts it as
missing (pandas' `isna`). `storage_test.zig` checks, array by array, that `FrameBuilder`
and `columnFromCells` build exactly what `dataset.Frame.fromDataset` builds.

**Categorical and duration columns (rows 100, 101; 2026-11-08, tests in
`src/catdur_test.zig`).** Both reuse a cell kind, as `.date` and `.timestamp` do, so no
`Value` arm is added: a categorical cell is `.text`, a duration cell an `.int` of
microseconds. A categorical column is dictionary-encoded where it is made (`cast`, `mutate`
with that `type`, the readers' `types`): `ColumnData.categorical`, one `u32` code per row and
the distinct values once, lexically ordered, so a code compares as its text and is pandas'
`cat.codes` (polars 2's physical codes follow first appearance; neither engine sorts by
them: both sort a categorical lexically, as here). Every verb that does not name the storage
reads it through `get` as text; `take` (so `filter`, `sort`, `head`, joins' payload) gathers
the codes and shares the dictionary, `concat` encodes the union again. A column declared
categorical may hold plain text storage (a `FrameBuilder` frame): it reads the same. Categories
in a given order (pandas `ordered=True`, polars `Enum`) are built (wave W6, below); group/join/sort
over the codes rather than the text (the speed of an encoded key) — Backlog, measured first. A duration is ISO 8601 in CSV and JSON
(`formatIsoDuration`, polars' JSON form; polars refuses a duration in CSV, pandas writes
`1 days 02:03:04`, which `parseDurationCell` reads too) and polars' `1d 2h` in `format`.
`mutate` gives an expression the temporal type it keeps (`expr.temporalType`: `ts - ts` a
duration, `ts ± dur` a timestamp, `dur * k` a duration, the `dt` functions that move an
instant its input's type), since the cells alone cannot tell an instant, a length and an int
apart.

**List and struct columns (rows 56, 94; 2026-11-08, tests in `src/nested_test.zig`).** Arrow's
layouts: `ColumnData.list` is `u32` offsets (rows + 1) into one element column (`items`, any
storage, nested again), `ColumnData.@"struct"` one child column per field with the field names
(behind a pointer, so a cell can point at it), each with its own validity bits. A cell is a
borrowed view, as `.text` is: `Value.list` (`ListView`: the element column and a range) and
`Value.record` (`RecordView`: the struct column and a row), 16 bytes each, so `Value` stays 32.
`Column.inner` declares the element column of a list and the fields of a struct (types only;
the storage holds the names that count), so an empty list column still has an element type
and the writers know an instant inside a list. Every structural verb carries nested columns:
`take` (so filter, sort, head, slices, joins' payload, `gatherEvery`) rebuilds the offsets and
gathers each level once through one index of element positions; `concat` and every verb that
builds from cells go through `ColBuilder`, which copies a nested cell's elements into storage
of the column's own (a `FrameBuilder` row too). Keys over them are free: `keys.encode` writes a
list as its length and elements and a record as its fields in order, so group, join, sort,
distinct and `value_counts` take list and struct keys with `Value.order`'s equality (polars'
lexicographic order, the shorter first; `[1]` equals `[1.0]`), where the design note had
planned `error.UnsupportedType`. Arithmetic, string and date functions give null on a nested
cell (as for bool); comparison is `Value.order`'s; `mutate` carries a nested result over with
its source's `inner`; `cast` to text writes its JSON. **Depth:** a nested value
`max_nesting_depth` (64, Arrow IPC's bound) levels down reads as null in every walker
(comparison, keys, gather, building, the writers), so a hand-built storage that points back at
itself ends there, never in a stack overflow; the logical size of a hand-built DAG shared many
times is the caller's, like a claimed `len`. A record of other field names than its column's
makes the column boxed (a mix), as an int among texts does.

**A result borrows from its input.** A verb shares every column it did not touch, and a
selection of all rows in order shares the columns outright; temporaries stay in the arena.
**Hand-built frames** with arrays shorter than `len`, fewer `data` entries than `columns`, a
short bitmap or text offsets out of order read as null there, never past an array's end.

**The verbs run `tabular`'s code.** `core.zig` (accumulators, predicate, window
aggregates) and `keys.zig` (canonical key encoding, seeded factorizer with a work cap,
radix sort) are `tabular`'s, with their imports changed. Where a verb needs rows (a key
that is not one plain int or text column, `pivot`, the rank path of `sort`) it builds a
row view of the key columns only, so key equality and ordering are `Value.order`'s in every
verb. Row indexes are `u32`: a frame of 2^32 - 1 rows or more is `error.TooLarge`.

**`cumsum` and `rolling` follow pandas and polars** (review 2026-11-07): they are `window`'s `.cum_sum` and `.rolling`, so a missing cell is skipped and its row is null, and a window short of values is null; an all-int `cumsum` stays int. The SIMD sum path `tabular.frame.rolling` had is gone with the row-verb rule (D4 measures).

**Elsewhere the semantics are still `tabular`'s historical defaults** (`skip_na = false`, an int `sum` is
a float). The plan decides pandas and polars semantics as the defaults; that switch is a D2
item in § Backlog, made once the row verbs are no longer the oracle for it.

## Limits and refusals

The same constants as `tabular`, refused with `error.TooLarge` before the work is done:
`max_aggregate_cells` 2^24 (groups x aggregates), `max_unpivot_cells` 2^22,
`max_pivot_cells` 2^22 (row keys x column keys), `max_join_cells` 2^24 (output rows x
columns), `max_rolling_work` 2^30 element visits; since wave W10 `max_bins` 2^20 breakpoints or labels
(`binIntervals`/`binQuantiles`/`binRanks`), and `unstack`/`wideToLong` results at `max_unpivot_cells`. Each is
pinned by a test in
`src/verbs_test.zig` against the row verb's refusal. Hash tables refuse past their work cap
(`keys.zig`), so constructed keys end in `TooLarge`, not a hang.

Added by the D5 sweep (`src/sweep_s1_test.zig`), all `error.TooLarge` unless said:
**row indexes** are `u32`, so every verb that builds them (all but the column-only ones)
calls `core.checkRowsU32(f.len)` at its entry, before it allocates: a frame of
`maxInt(u32)` rows or more is refused. Only a hand-built `Frame` can claim that many rows.
`pivotMany`, `pivotKeys`: all value blocks together hold at most `max_pivot_cells` cells (one
block was capped before, so `values.len` blocks were `values.len` times the cap).
`dummies`: all encoded columns together at most `max_aggregate_cells` cells, a column named
twice in `cols` included. A verb that pads a shorter frame to a taller one (`arith`,
`combineFirst`, `concat(.horizontal)`) creates at most `max_join_cells` cells beyond the
cells of its inputs (`verbs.growthWithin`). A `Selector` visits at most
`max_selector_visits` (4096) nodes per column, a node shared by several parents counted
each time (`error.BadArgument`, as for a depth past `max_selector_depth`). Name lookups for
many names build one hash index (`frame.NameIndex`, `verbs.Names`) instead of scanning
the columns per name: a frame of millions of columns is one `pivot` or `transpose` away.

**Nested columns (2026-11-08):** a list column holds at most `maxInt(u32)` elements in all (Arrow's
`u32` offsets; `take` past it `error.TooLarge`, a builder `error.OutOfMemory`, `readJson` `TooManyCells`
long before); a nested value `max_nesting_depth` (64) levels down reads as null, and `readJson` keeps it as
its JSON text.

**D5 sweep (2026-11-08), expression, window and name limits.** `max_rolling_work` and
`max_window_work` bound the work of the *whole call*, summed over every partition (`rolling`
window x rows, `expanding` and `rolling_time` prefix per row), refused before any partition is
computed where the sum is known from the partition sizes. They count element *visits*, not
their cost: a window `quantile`, `median` or `nunique` also selects or sorts its `w` values per
row, so the time for the same cap is a log factor (about 20x at `w` = 2^20) larger than for
`sum`. `max_eval_bytes` (2^30) bounds what the cells of one `mutate` assignment or one `where`
allocate while they are evaluated (`repeat`, `pad`, `replace`, text results...), past it
`error.TooLarge`; `max_text_result` still bounds one cell. Substring search on a needle of more
than 64 bytes (`contains`, `find`, `rfind`, `count_matches` between two columns) is O(text +
needle); shorter needles use `std.mem` (O(text x 64)). Resolving the names of a spec
(`partition_by`, `subset`, `cols`, `by`, `describe`'s columns, `concatByName`'s and
`joinAsof`'s output) is one hash lookup per name, not a scan of the columns. `readCsvReader`
holds the stream in `a` while it grows (`allocRemaining` doubles, and an arena keeps every
block), so with an arena its peak is up to about 3 x `max_bytes` before the frame is built;
`max_bytes` is the dial, or read into a slice you own and call `readCsv`.

**Callback verbs and window rank/corr/cov (2026-11-08).** `rollingMap` hands at most
`max_rolling_map_work` (= `max_rolling_work`, 2^30) cells to its callbacks in one call, summed
over partitions and refused before the first call; `rolling_rank` counts `rows x window` visits
(an expanding one `rows^2`), `rolling_corr`/`rolling_cov` `2 x rows x window`, against
`max_window_work` per call like the other window functions. `mapGroups` adds up its results' rows
before it copies any and creates at most `max_join_cells` cells beyond its input
(`verbs.growthWithin`), so a callback frame claiming 2^25 rows of no storage is `error.TooLarge`
at once.

**No-panic sweep of the S2 code (2026-11-10).** The names a `split_fields` makes count against `max_nodes` (one at its widest, 4096, costs 4096 of 65,536; fuzz seed 493021). `max_nodes` bounds the nodes of one expression
*including* the bodies of `list_eval`, `list_filter` and `struct_fields` (one budget for the whole
tree; a node reached twice through a shared parent counts twice), else `error.ExprTooLarge`. The
schema walks over an expression (nested list/struct types, temporal type, zone) run only after
`go` has bounded the operand and are linear in it. `corr`/`cov`: the result matrix holds at most
`max_corr_cells` (2^26 cells, 8192 columns) whatever the rows, else `error.TooLarge`.
`cumFoldColumns`/`cumSumHorizontal` build at most `max_join_cells` cells beyond the frame's own (a
column named twice in `cols` is built twice). `repeatValue` weighs a nested value by every text
byte and element it holds, down to `max_nesting_depth`, against `max_repeat_bytes`.
`NdjsonChunkReader` keeps no blank line, so a stream of blank lines costs no memory.

## Input and output (D3)

**Where:** `src/csvio.zig` (`readCsv`, `readCsvReader`, `writeCsv`), `src/jsonio.zig` (`writeJson`,
`writeNdjson`), `src/render.zig` (`format`, `toMarkdown`), cell spellings in `src/textio.zig`.
CSV goes through the sibling `csvstream` (the module's second production dependency, with
`datefmt`): it cuts records and fields and writes the quoting; this module has no CSV parser.

**`readCsv(a, bytes, CsvReadOptions)`** reads the input twice through one record scanner: the
first pass types each column from *all* its cells (pandas does the same; polars samples 100
rows), the second builds the columns, so no cell is kept in between. `readCsvReader` takes a
`std.Io.Reader` and reads at most `max_bytes` of it first. Options: `delimiter`, `quote` (0 =
off), `has_header` (off: columns `column_0`, `column_1`... as polars 2.1), `names`, `columns`
(subset, in file order as pandas' `usecols`), `types` (per-name `TypeOverride`, a cell that
does not parse is `error.BadValue`), `null_values`, `infer_types` (off: all text), `parse_dates`,
`skip_rows`, `n_rows`, `comment`, `truncate_ragged`, `strict_quotes` and the limits below.

**Inference order** (each token, after the null markers): `int` = `[+-]digits` fitting i64 with
blanks around it allowed (pandas; polars takes neither `+` nor blanks); `float` = decimal or
exponent form, `inf`/`infinity`/`nan` in any case (pandas; polars `inf` and `NaN` only); `bool` =
`true`/`false` in any case; with `parse_dates` (off by default in both engines) `date` for
`YYYY-MM-DD` and `timestamp` for the other ISO 8601 forms (zones applied, result UTC; a column
mixing the two is text, both engines); else `text`. Where the engines disagree, the vectors
carry a label and the engine followed:

| case | pandas | polars | here |
|---|---|---|---|
| null markers | 19 strings (`pandas_na_values`), a quoted `NA` too | only `""` (`polars_na_values`) | pandas' list, `null_values` replaces it |
| int column with a missing cell | float64 with NaN | Int64 with null | int with a null (polars) |
| integer past int64 | uint64 / object | Int128 | text (a float would lose digits) |
| column of nothing but nulls | float64 | String | text (polars) |
| blank line | skipped | a row of nulls | skipped (csvstream) |
| repeated / empty header name | `a.1`, `Unnamed: 1` (skipping names the header holds) | `a_duplicated_0`, `` | pandas |
| short row | padded with NaN | padded with null | padded with null; a long row is `error.RaggedRow` unless `truncate_ragged` (both engines refuse) |
| quote inside an unquoted field | literal | error | literal (csvstream) |
| `Infinity`, `INF`, `nan`, ` 4`, `+3` | float / int | text | float / int (pandas) |

**Defaults decided (2026-11-08, owner left the call to the maintainer):** `parse_dates` stays off (both
engines; a column that merely looks like a date is not silently retyped), an integer past i64 stays text (no
digit is lost; a caller who wants a float asks with `types`), and `writeJson` keeps RFC 3339 `…Z` timestamps
(unambiguous and zone-explicit, where pandas' epoch milliseconds lose the type and polars' form drops the zone).

**`writeCsv(a, w, frame, CsvWriteOptions)`** writes pandas' spelling: floats as Python's `repr`
(`1.0`, `1e-05`, `inf`; NaN is the null text), bools `True`/`False` (`true_text`, `false_text`),
dates as ISO text, timestamps `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` with a 3- or 6-digit fraction on every cell
of a column when one cell has a fraction (pandas), decimals exact, `\n` line ends (`line_terminator`),
`float_precision` rounding the exact binary value as `%.Nf` does (`2.675` to two digits is
`2.67`). Quoting: `necessary`, `always`, `never`, `non_numeric`; an empty *text* is written
`""` (polars; pandas writes nothing, which reads back as null) and so is a lone empty field.
Differences from the engines, all labelled in the vectors: bools (polars `true`), tiny floats
(polars `0.00001`), NaN (polars `NaN`), timestamps (polars ISO with `T`), a lone null (polars
writes an empty line a reader skips).

**`writeJson(w, frame, .records | .columns)`** and **`writeNdjson`**: compact; a list is an array and a
record an object with its field names (an int inside as a timestamp or duration where `Column.inner` says so);
`writeCsv` writes a nested cell as that JSON text (pandas writes a Python repr, polars refuses), and `format`
and `toMarkdown` show it, cut like any long cell (polars prints `[1, 2]` and `{1,"a"}`). The number and string
rules are `dataset.frameToJson`'s (NaN and infinities `null`, invalid UTF-8 replaced by U+FFFD) with
floats keeping a fractional digit (`1.0`, both engines) and timestamps as RFC 3339 `…Z` text (pandas:
epoch milliseconds, polars: `2021-01-02 03:04:05`). `columns` is pandas' `orient="list"`, not its
index-keyed `"columns"` (there is no index). The tests compare the parsed documents, so number
spelling (`1e-05` against `0.00001`) is free.

**Options added in S2 (2026-11-09).** Which engine each follows; where the engines differ the vectors carry a
label (`oracle3_io_vectors.json`: 14 `read-s2-*`, 9 `write-csv-s2-*` cases, 13 byte-for-byte `to_json` option
cases, 8 `to_html` and 3 `glimpse` cases).

- **`readCsv`:** `thousands` (pandas; polars has none) and `decimal` (pandas; polars `decimal_comma` is
  `decimal = ','`) rewrite a cell only for the numeric reading: a column that is not all numbers keeps its text, and with a
  decimal comma a `.` is not a number. `true_values`/`false_values` (pandas): a column whose cells are all among them and
  `true`/`false` is bool; an entry wins over a number (`1`/`0`). `extra_null_values` (pandas `na_values` with
  `keep_default_na=True`: the default list is `null_values`' default; `keep_default_na=False` is `null_values = &.{}`, so there is no
  flag), `column_null_values` (pandas dict `na_values`, polars per-column `null_values`, both add to the global ones; a name
  the file lacks is `NoSuchColumn`), `na_filter = false` (no null at all), `empty_string_is_null = false` (the empty cell is
  an empty text; polars `missing_utf8_is_empty_string`, which the pinned polars does not have, so pandas is the oracle).
  `skipinitialspace` (pandas; csvstream `Trim.leading`, so a quote after the blanks opens a field), `skipfooter` (pandas;
  counted in records), `skip_rows_after_header` (polars; with `has_header = false` it drops the first data row), `row_index_name`/
  `row_index_offset` (polars; an `int` column in front, `BadOptions` when the name is taken), `on_bad_lines = .skip` with
  `bad_lines_skipped` (pandas: a record with too many fields; `n_rows` counts kept rows), `date_format` (pandas
  `date_format`: a `%` layout through `dtfn.translateFormat`/`strptime`, `date` unless it names a time of day;
  pandas' `dayfirst` is `"%d/%m/%Y"` here, there is no guessing; no `parse_dates` means no effect, except on a
  `.date`/`.timestamp` entry of `types`), `escape_char`/`double_quote` (pandas `escapechar`/`doublequote`; polars has
  neither; `quote = 0` is `QUOTE_NONE`). `thousands == decimal` or `decimal = 0` is `BadOptions`. Everything above
  except the last three rewrites cells, so a read with `thousands`, `decimal`, `true_values`/`false_values`,
  `column_null_values` or `date_format` takes the cell-by-cell pass-1/pass-2 reader and not the speculative one-pass
  reader (the typed fast path is untouched for every other read).
- **`writeCsv`:** `date_format` (`.date`) and `datetime_format` (`.timestamp`, UTC) as `%` layouts (pandas
  `date_format`, polars `date_format`/`datetime_format`), `float_scientific` (polars: `true` is Rust's `1.2345e3`, with
  `float_precision` digits when set; `false` never an exponent, `2` for 2.0 as polars prints it; `null` Python's `repr`),
  `columns` (pandas; a missing name is `NoSuchColumn`), `decimal` (pandas; polars `decimal_comma`), `include_bom`
  (polars), `double_quote = false` with `escape_char` (pandas: Python leaves a field bare when only its quote needs
  escaping, csvstream quotes it, `"q\"x"`; both read back the same, labelled in the vectors).
- **JSON write:** `writeJsonOpts(a, w, f, orient, JsonWriteOptions)`; `writeJson(w, f, orient)` is unchanged and compact.
  `JsonOrient` gained `split`, `index`, `values`, `table` (pandas shapes with the default `RangeIndex` 0..n-1; the
  Table Schema carries `pandas_version` `"1.4.0"`); `force_ascii` (pandas, default *on* there, off here: valid UTF-8 as
  before; escaped in this file rather than through `jsontext`'s `ascii_only`, which would make `jsontext` a dependency for
  fifteen lines), `double_precision` (pandas, at most 15), `indent` (pandas, ujson's layout: `"a":1` without a space; the
  document is built compact in memory first, capped by `max_indent_bytes` -> `OutputTooLarge`), `date_format = .epoch` with
  `date_unit` (pandas; a date is its midnight UTC, a duration a count of the unit).
- **JSON read:** `JsonReadOrient` gained `split` (`columns` found by its own scan, so key order is free; a row longer than
  `columns` is `BadShape`), `index` (keys dropped), `values` (columns `column_0`...), `table` (the `primaryKey` columns
  dropped, as pandas makes them the index); `epoch_dates` + `date_unit` (pandas `convert_dates=[...]`, `date_unit`: integer
  columns become `timestamp`; no guessing by column name).
- **`toHtml`/`htmlTo`** (pandas `to_html(index=False)`: the layout is byte for byte pandas' for ints, text, bools, floats and
  nulls, 8 vectors; `null_text` default `NaN`, `float_precision`, `border` (0 omits it, as pandas), extra `classes`, `header`,
  `escape` (also escapes `"`, which pandas leaves)) and **`glimpse`/`glimpseTo`** (polars `glimpse` as its string form
  prints it, 3 vectors: names padded, `<type>` right-aligned, text in single quotes, `max_items` values, no line cut unless
  `max_width` is set).

**`readJson(a, bytes, JsonReadOptions)`** (`.records`, `.columns`) and **`readNdjson`** (2026-11-08) are the
reverse, through `std.json.Scanner` in two passes (zig-libs has no JSON module of its own; `json5` is a
superset parser for config files): columns in the order their keys first appear, each typed by `readCsv`'s
rules on the same text (`csvio.parseAs` does both, so `1`, `1.5`, `true` and, with `parse_dates`, ISO dates
and instants read as they do from CSV). Nested values (2026-11-08): a column of arrays only is a `list`
column, of objects only a `struct` column (one field per key any object has, null where one lacks it, in
first-seen order), each element and field typed by the same rules, down to `max_nesting_depth` — polars'
reading; pandas keeps Python objects. A column that mixes kinds (an array among numbers, arrays and objects)
or holds an integer past i64 is text, each cell its JSON source (`1`, `true`, `{"a":[1,2]}`), at every level
the same (a list of `1` and `"x"` is a list of text), and so is a value nested past the bound: the source
text loses nothing. A missing key is null (both engines). **A key repeated in one object, at any depth, is
`error.BadJson` by default** (`duplicate_keys = .reject`, `jsonshape`'s default and reasoning: two parsers of
one feed can disagree on it; until 2026-11-08 the last value won); `.last` keeps the last value (Python's
`json`, so pandas), a repeated `columns` key its last array, and the field's type then follows every value
the key had. `columns` arrays of different lengths are `error.RaggedColumns` (both engines refuse). ndjson
skips blank lines and takes `\r\n`. Options: `columns`, `types` (as `readCsv`'s; a nested value reads as text,
its source, or as the nested kind it is), `parse_dates` (inside nested values too), `n_rows` (the rest must
still be JSON), `duplicate_keys`, limits `max_bytes`, `max_columns` (distinct key paths: columns, their fields and list elements together),
`max_cell_bytes` (strings, numbers, keys, a nested value's text), `max_rows`, `max_cells` (every cell the
frame holds: rows x columns plus every element and every field slot, a null row's included). The column walk
is iterative; inside a nested value it recurses at most `max_nesting_depth` levels, and a 100 000-deep value
is a test. What `writeJson`/`writeNdjson` write reads back `equals` the frame (timestamps with `parse_dates`;
a decimal column reads back as float unless `types` says `.decimal`, as JSON numbers carry no scale), nested
columns included (`src/nested_test.zig`, and the fuzz harness's `json_read` target). **Not here, by design:**
JSONPath queries, projection of deep documents and `json_normalize`-style flattening are `jsonshape`'s (RFC
9535 engine, column key paths, depth and work limits; it returns `dataset` until step R repoints it at
`Frame`); this module only builds the nested columns a document has. `dataframe` cannot depend on
`jsonshape` (a cycle after step R). Tests in `src/jsonread_test.zig`, `src/nested_test.zig`.

**`format(a, frame, FormatOptions)`** is `to_string(index=False)` (right-aligned columns, one space
between) cut like polars' `__repr__`: `max_rows` 10 and `max_cols` 12 keep the first and last half
around a `…` row and column, a cell past `max_cell_chars` 32 ends in `…`, `null_text` "null",
`show_dtypes`, `show_shape`. **`toMarkdown`** is a pipe table laid out as `tabulate` does for
pandas (numbers right-aligned, a column two wider than its header; `tabulate`'s decimal-point
alignment of floats is not done; `|` and newlines in a cell are escaped). Neither has an engine
oracle: pandas' `to_string` pads floats to a common number of decimals and `to_markdown` needs
`tabulate`, which the pinned venv lacks; `src/io_test.zig` pins the layout by hand.

**Chunked reading (S2 wave W9, 2026-11-09).** `CsvChunkReader` (`src/csvchunk.zig`; pandas
`read_csv(chunksize=n)` / `iterator=True` + `get_chunk(n)`, polars `read_csv_batched` + `next_batches(n)`):
`init(gpa, reader, CsvReadOptions, ChunkOptions)`, `next(a, n) !?Frame` (null at the end), `deinit`. The reader
holds a byte window of one read plus one record and the queued records of one chunk, never the stream:
`max_bytes` caps one chunk's text, `max_record_bytes` one record (`RecordTooLarge`), `max_rows`/`max_cells` one
chunk. There is no CSV scanning of its own: records are cut with csvstream's `SpanScanner`/`LineIterator`
configured as `readCsv` configures them (`csvio.recordSpanConfig`), and the next `n` records, behind the header,
go through `readCsv` itself, so cells, null markers, quoting and every limit read as in a whole read. The
differential test (`s2w9_test.zig`) holds that: for every chunk size and a stream handing out 1..7 bytes per
call, the chunks end to end equal `readCsv` cell by cell. The stream is read as it comes (`fill(1)`), the
rescan of a long unfinished record is geometric, so a record of M bytes costs O(M).
`ChunkOptions.schema`: `.first_chunk` (default, polars) fixes `types` where given and infers the rest from the
first chunk, or from `infer_rows` rows (polars `infer_schema_length`; the rows read ahead wait for the next call),
and keeps the types; a later cell that does not parse is `error.BadValue` with `error_line` the 1-based input
line (polars raises too); `ignore_errors` (polars) nulls the cell instead, if a null marker exists to write.
`.per_chunk` is pandas: each chunk is inferred alone, so a column can change type between chunks (documented
there, pandas does the same). Across chunks: the header is read once; `skip_rows`, `skip_rows_after_header`,
`comment`, BOM, quoted newlines across a read boundary, `on_bad_lines = .skip` (a skipped record is not one of
the `n` rows; `bad_lines_skipped` is the running total), `n_rows` (the stream's total) and `row_index_offset`
(continues) work as in `readCsv`. Differences kept on purpose: a stream with a header and no rows yields no chunk
(polars `next_batches` returns nothing; pandas yields one empty chunk with the header's columns), the error kind for an unterminated quote that swallows the rest can be `RecordTooLarge` where a
whole read says `UnterminatedQuote`, and a header-less file's width is the first record's. Refused:
`skipfooter` is `error.UnsupportedOption` (it needs the end of the input; pandas' C engine refuses it with
`chunksize` too). `NdjsonChunkReader` (`src/ndjsonchunk.zig`; pandas `read_json(lines=True, chunksize=n)`; polars
has no public chunked ndjson reader: `read_ndjson`'s `batch_size` only sizes internal batches) cuts lines and
hands the next `n` non-blank ones to `readNdjson`; each chunk is typed on its own with the keys it has, as in
pandas (a cross-chunk schema would have to decide what a key one chunk lacks means, which no engine defines for
ndjson), and `types` fixes a column in every chunk. Engine answers: `tools/oracle2h.py`, `src/s2w9_oracle_test.zig`.


**Wave W10 (dataframe S2, 2026-11-10): the cheap parity gaps.** Seven items the survey found "missing and it
matters"; each was asked of the engines first (`tools/oracle2i.py`, 231 cases, replayed by
`src/s2w10_oracle_test.zig`; the edge cases no engine is asked are in `src/s2w10_test.zig`).
- **`Expr.find_regex`** (polars `str.find(pattern, literal=False)`): the **byte** offset of the first match
  (polars' unit, not the character index of pandas/Python `str.find`, which is also literal and answers -1),
  null when there is none or the cell is not text; an invalid pattern is `error.BadPattern` (`strict=True`).
  `literal` quotes the pattern (`regex.quoteMetaAlloc`). Same plumbing and linear-time guarantee as
  `contains_regex`/`extract`.
- **`corrWith(left, right, {method, drop})`** (pandas `DataFrame.corrwith`, `axis=0`): columns named in both
  frames correlated by row position; no row index here, so frames of different length are
  `error.LengthMismatch` (pandas aligns on the index), and `other` is a frame, never a Series. The result is
  `column` + `corr`: shared columns in the left frame's order, then (unless `drop`) the one-sided ones sorted by
  name with a null (pandas NaN). A shared text column is `error.NotNumeric` (pandas `TypeError`). Spearman is
  checked against pandas' `DataFrame.corr(method="spearman")` of the two columns side by side (corrwith's own
  needs SciPy, not installed). The arithmetic is `corr.zig`'s (complete pairs, `pearson`, `rankAverage`); work
  capped by `max_corr_work`.
- **`Expr.json_encode`** (polars `struct.json_encode()`): the record's JSON through `jsonio.writeValue`, the
  writer the cast to text and the JSON writers share (no second encoder). With a column reference the declared
  schema is used (an instant inside stays RFC 3339). A null struct cell gives the text `null`, as polars; a cell
  that is not a record is null (polars `SchemaError`). Kept difference: polars writes `1e-7`, the shared writer
  `1e-07` (both valid JSON). Result text over `max_text_result` is `error.TooLarge`.
- **`unstack(step, how, columns, fill_value / fill_values)`** (polars `DataFrame.unstack`): `.vertical` and
  `.horizontal`, the `<name>_<k>` names zero-padded to the width of the largest `k`, types kept, a scalar fill
  (`fill_value`) or one per column (`fill_values`, a wrong count is an error as in polars), cast to the column's
  type as polars does. An empty frame or `step = 0` is `error.BadArgument` (polars raises a Python error); the
  result is capped at `max_unpivot_cells` cells (`error.TooLarge`; polars would allocate any `step`); a column
  listed twice is `error.DuplicateColumn`.
- **`wideToLong(stubnames, i, j, sep, suffix)`** (pandas `wide_to_long`): an unpivot of the columns
  `<stub><sep><suffix>` (the `regex` module's Rust grammar for `suffix`, the stub and separator quoted) into one
  value column per stub. pandas' (`i`, `j`) index is ordinary columns: `i...`, `j`, the other columns, the stubs.
  Row order and the `j` typing are pandas' (one `i` column: all rows of the first suffix, then the next; several:
  each source row's suffixes together; `j` int, else float, else text; suffixes in order of first appearance).
  Differences: a suffix a stub lacks is null in an unchanged-type column (pandas turns an int column into float
  with NaN; an int and a float column of one stub make a float one here too); the other columns keep frame order
  (pandas uses a set, so its order changes between runs); a stub with no column is `error.NoSuchColumn`
  (pandas returns an empty frame), an `i` that repeats is `error.NotUnique` (pandas `ValueError`), a stub of
  mixed non-numeric types `error.BadArgument`, `j` naming a column `error.DuplicateColumn`; the result is capped
  at `max_unpivot_cells` cells.
- **`binIntervals` / `binQuantiles` / `binRanks`** (polars 2.1 `Expr.bin_intervals` / `bin_quantiles` /
  `bin_ranks`; they exist in 2.1.0, marked experimental), as frame verbs like `cut`: `col`, `out`, a list of
  breakpoints / quantiles / rank fractions or a count of bins, `labels` (one per bin, else the bin number as an
  int; text here where polars has an `Enum`), `include_intervals` (a record `{bin, left, right}` with open outer
  ends) and `right_closed` (not for ranks). Quantile breakpoints are values at `floor(q * (n - 1))` (a count `k`: in
  integer arithmetic); rank cuts are at `round(r * n)` positions in stable sorted order (a count: near-equal bins,
  the remainder to the first ones), so equal values can split; derived equal-width breakpoints of an int-like
  column are rounded to the side that keeps the bins' integers those of the exact ones (up for `[a, b)`, down
  for `(a, b]`). Differences: NaN is missing (this module's one rule) and gets no bin, polars bins it last
  and counts it; the bin count is capped at `max_bins` (2^20, `error.TooLarge`); columns are `int`, `float`,
  `timestamp`, `duration`, `date`, `text` (quantiles and a count: numeric only), others `error.NotOrderable`;
  `error.BadEdges` for decreasing breakpoints or fractions, fractions outside [0, 1], a count of 0, and
  `error.BadLabels` for a label count that is not the bin count or a repeated label.
- **`offset_by` on a zoned column**: the calendar units (`mo`, `q`, `y`, `w`, `d`) move the wall clock of the
  zone (`1d` keeps 12:00 across a DST change, an elapsed 23 or 25 hours) and the sub-day part (`h`, `m`, `s`, `ms`,
  `us`, `ns`) is added as elapsed time after it (`1d1h`), as polars (this changes the previous elapsed-time result
  for calendar units; `dtfn.offsetByZoned`). A wall-clock result the zone skips is `local - offset after the
  gap` (02:30 in a 02:00 to 03:00 jump is 01:30; polars, unlike `truncate`'s forward move); one it shows twice
  is the pass the input was in (the same UTC offset), the earlier one if the input's offset is neither. `Duration`
  gained `days` (calendar days given, a week as seven). A column whose `time_zone` `tz` does not know makes
  `offset_by` `error.BadExpr` at compile time, as `truncate` and the other zone readers (it was elapsed time
  before W10; review W10R-3). `add_business_days` on a zoned column was not asked of the engines and is
  not built (it still works on the instant as before).

**Wave W11 (dataframe S2, 2026-11-10): real dtype widths.** The owner chose real width types over names checked as
ranges (2026-11-10): `ColumnType` `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `uint8`, `uint16`, `uint32`, `uint64`, `float32` beside
`int` (Int64) and `float` (Float64), each with its own array. Engines asked first (`tools/oracle2j.py`, 6113 cases of
polars 2.1 and pandas 3.1, replayed by `src/s2w11_oracle_test.zig` (cast, read, write), `src/s2w11a_oracle_test.zig`
(arithmetic, literals, unary, aggregates, combining) and `src/s2w11b_oracle_test.zig` (keys, sort, unique, group by,
type names); plain tests `src/s2w11_test.zig`, `src/s2w11a_test.zig`, `src/s2w11b_test.zig` (a sweep of every verb over
a frame of all eight widths)). Design in one place: `src/dtype.zig` (predicates, ranges, `supertype`).
- **Storage follows a declared width** (for `int`/`float` it still follows the cells): `frame.conform` gives a
  width column its array, a cell the width does not hold becoming null; every builder, reader, `cast`, `mutate`
  and verb result passes through it, and `frame.widthsConform` is checked on every verb result by the fuzz
  harness. A width cell reads as `Value.int` / `Value.float` (exact); a UInt64 above `maxInt(i64)` as the new
  `Value.uint`, which orders, compares, keys (one key with an equal float or decimal), sorts and joins by its
  exact value.
- **Types of results** follow polars: a binary arithmetic node is the supertype of its operands, computed from the
  schema before any cell (`expr.numType`, at most 4096 nodes walked); an integer literal is weak (`i8 + 1` is Int8,
  `i8 + 128` Int16); `/` per polars' table; `sum`/`cum_sum`/`prod` of Int8/Int16/UInt8/UInt16 are Int64, of
  Int32/UInt32/UInt64/Float32/Int64 their own type; mean-like aggregates of a Float32 are Float32; `diff` of an
  unsigned type the next wider signed one; concat, `if_else`, `coalesce` meet in the supertype. Unary minus of an
  unsigned column is `error.BadExpr` (polars raises).
- **`cast`** to a width checks the range (out of it: null, `error.CastFailed` with `.fail`); `CastSpec.on_error`
  gains `.wrap` (polars `wrap_numerical`, numpy `astype`): an integer wraps, a float saturates, NaN is 0.
- **I/O**: inference stays Int64/Float64 (both engines); `types` accepts the widths, a value out of range is
  `error.BadValue` (polars' `read_csv`); a Float32 cell is written as its shortest f32 digits (`0.1`), a UInt64 as
  its digits; type names in `info`/`show_dtypes` are polars' short ones (`i8` … `u64`, `f32`).
- **Differences kept, each with its reason in the replay's `known` list:** an integer result outside its type is
  **null** (both engines wrap; the module's Int64 rule before W11); Int64 or a narrower signed type with UInt64
  meets in **Float64** (polars Int128, which this module does not have; pandas float64); NaN stays missing (a NaN
  cast is null); `readJson` reads a typed cell as `readCsv` reads its text (polars' `read_json` casts leniently);
  joins accept keys of any two numeric types by exact value (polars refuses Int64 with Float64), the key keeping the
  left type and widening to the supertype when a right-only key does not fit it; `n_unique`/counts stay Int64 (polars
  UInt32); Float32 aggregates add in f64 and round once (within one f32 ulp of polars); the bin verbs give Int64/Float64
  interval ends. **Changed for Int64 with W11:** `aggregate` `sum`/`prod` of an Int64 column storing ints is Int64,
  exact in an `i128`, null on overflow (it was Float64, so 2^53 + 1 was lost; the engines' answer).
- Not part of W11: Int128, Binary, fixed-size Array and a time-of-day type.

**Limits** (all `CsvReadOptions` fields, each with its own error; a hostile input is an error, never
a panic or an unbounded allocation): `max_bytes` 256 MiB (`InputTooLarge`), `max_columns` 65536
(`TooManyColumns`), `max_cell_bytes` 1 MiB (`CellTooLarge`), `max_record_bytes` 16 MiB
(`RecordTooLarge` for a line; a quoted field still open at the cap is `UnterminatedQuote`),
`max_rows` 2^26 (`TooManyRows`), `max_cells` 2^26 (`TooManyCells`). An unterminated quote is
`UnterminatedQuote` (or, with `strict_quotes` off, a literal quote). `max_quoted_lines`: under
`strict_quotes` no line cap (so every cell `writeCsv` writes reads back); without it
csvstream's 64, because each stray quote then looks ahead that far (a larger cap multiplies
the scan). Memory: the input, the header names once per pass (three copies), one `Value`
row, and the frame -- 8 to 16 bytes per cell plus text, so at `max_cells` a frame of ints is
~0.5 GiB whatever the input's size; text reservations are capped at each column's share of
the input (review 2026-11-07 H1); the one-pass reader reserves its rows only when rows x
columns fits the input's length (+ 4096 cells), else the two-pass reader, which counts the rows
it really has, runs (sweep S2-1: blank lines, comments or quoted newlines no longer reserve a
row each). The table `hostile input answers errors` in
`src/io_test.zig` pins each limit.

**D5 sweep S2 (2026-11-08), closed** (`src/sweep_s2_test.zig`; files `expr exprfn window more
analysis csvio jsonio textio render dtfn seriesfn`): S2-1 the one-pass CSV reader reserved a
row per newline for every column, ~2000x the input with blank lines over a wide header; S2-2
the window work cap was per partition (summed over partitions it was unbounded); S2-3
`fillNull` kept input validity bits past the last row; S2-4 `mutate`/`where` text results had
no total bound (`repeat` over a column of 1 MiB cells); S2-5 `contains` and friends between two
columns were O(text x needle); S2-6 name resolution against a wide frame (`concatByName`,
`joinAsof` suffix scan, `fillNull`/`duplicateMask`/... subsets, `window` `partition_by`,
`describe`, `partitionBy`, `valueCounts`) was width x width; S2-7 the `is_in` key length was an
unchecked `@intCast` to u32. `readCsv`'s `unreachable` on `SpeculationFailed` is now a fall
back to the cell path. Every other pub entry point of these files was walked and is clean;
operators over extreme cells and the writers over
extreme values are pinned by "sweep clean probe" tests. **Open (LOW, no panic):**
`exprfn.reverse`/`translate` free their `charStarts` after a later allocation (an arena keeps
8 bytes per character per cell, linear in the input); `formatTo` with `max_rows` of
`maxInt` over a hand-built frame claiming a huge `len` runs out of memory instead of
refusing; `replace_many`/`contains_any` patterns are quadratic in text x pattern (the
patterns are the caller's expression, not cell data).

**Review 2026-11-07 (third, D3), closed:** H1 text reservations of a wide first row over short
rows (~1000x the input), M1 a `writeCsv` cell of more than 64 lines did not read back, M2 the
two false claims above, L2 `markdownTo` `f.len + 1` on a hand-built frame, L3 a cut where the
text stops being UTF-8 split a code point, L9 a `.decimal` override refused zeros past 12
fraction digits, L10 pass 1 now types a float with the parse pass 2 uses; plus `format` caps
at `maxInt` (head half `n + 1`). Tests in `src/io_test.zig`. **Open (LOW, no panic):**
`max_cell_chars` cuts before control bytes are escaped (a cut cell can print 4x wider);
`writeCsv` has no `comment` option, so a first-column text starting with the reader's
`comment` byte is dropped on read (csvstream's `WriteOptions.comment` could be passed
through); a one-column frame written with `quote = 0` or `.never` turns a null into a blank
line the reader skips; timestamps outside years 0000-9999 are written in the expanded form
`parseIsoTimestamp` does not read; `textio.formatFloatFixed` falls back to shortest digits
above ~1.8e16 at 22 decimals (not C's `%.Nf`); `markdownTo` holds a copy of every cell.

## Verification

- `src/verbs_test.zig` — the verbs on hand-built frames: shared columns, bitmaps and arrays shorter
  than `len`, typed paths and their limits, the caps. (Until step R, 2026-11-08, it also ran every
  verb against `tabular`'s row verb over generated tables; that module is retired.)
- `src/oracle_test.zig` — all 1353 pandas/polars cases of `tabular`'s file, every one run;
  the known differences are listed in the file and must still differ.
- `src/more_test.zig` — the `u32` row limit and `concatByName`'s cell cap of the `more.zig` verbs.
- `src/structure_test.zig`, `src/analysis_test.zig`, `src/exprfn_test.zig` — the D2
  verbs (rows the row verbs never had, so no differential oracle) on hand-built tables,
  expected cells from pandas' and polars' documentation, numpy's quantile methods and
  Python's `str` (pandas and polars were not installed on the host: not run against them
  yet, an item for D5's oracle).
- `src/oracle3_io_test.zig` — `oracle3_io_vectors.json`: every `read_csv` case (types, cells, names,
  errors), every `to_csv`/`write_csv` text byte for byte, and the JSON documents, against what
  pandas 3.1.0 and polars 2.1.0 answered; `src/io_test.zig` — the hand-written cases: options,
  the hostile-input table, the round trip `writeCsv` to `readCsv` over every column kind, the
  rendering layout, `src/textio.zig` — the float spelling against Python's `repr`.
- `src/step4_test.zig` — the callback verbs (every shape, the error paths, the caps) and window
  `rolling_rank`/`rolling_corr`/`rolling_cov`, expected values from pandas' docstrings or by hand.
- `src/storage_test.zig` — storage against `columnFromCells` and the input rows, hand-built frames;
  `src/value_test.zig` — the cell model's own tests from `dataset` and a property sweep.

`testkit` is the only `test_dep`. The `dataset`/`tabular` differential is gone (step R,
2026-11-08); the anchors are the pandas/polars vectors, the `*Cells` reference paths and the
fuzz driver.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class C · oracle n/a

- **Class C** — an internal data structure and verb library; no wire format others must agree with.
- **Oracle n/a** — class C/D carries no anchor debt.

**What the tests actually contain.** What pandas 3.1.0 and polars 2.1.0 answered, frozen
(`src/oracle_vectors.json`, filtered by `tools/filter_vectors.py` from what `tools/oracle.py`
writes — `tabular`'s oracle, moved here with step R), what they answered for the D2 verbs
(`src/oracle2_vectors.json`, `tools/oracle2.py`, replayed by `src/oracle2_test.zig`: where
they disagree the vector says which one is followed, and the differences kept on purpose
are the test's `known` list: non-padded numeric fields in `strptime` (`datefmt`), a missing text in the `is*` classes
(null here, False in pandas' Arrow-backed `str` dtype), the `sum` of an int pivot column as a
float, `skew`/`kurt` of a group with no spread (0 here and in `tabular`, NaN in both
engines), and polars' `peak_min`/`peak_max` at the ends of a column, where 2.1.0 compares
the end cell with 0), and `tabular`'s row verbs as a re-derived oracle on generated tables.

**S2 wave W2 (2026-11-09), the everyday single-parameter gaps — built, with the engine each follows.**
pandas 3.1 unless said (`src/s2w2_test.zig` by hand; the engine cases in `tools/oracle2.py` groups `w2_*`, replayed by
`oracle2_test.zig`): `describeWith` (`percentiles`, `include`/`exclude` by type, `all`, text/bool/categorical
`count unique top freq`, timestamp and duration columns as ISO text; pandas prints exactly the percentiles asked, its
documented "median always" is not so in 3.1; `std` moves last beside a timestamp column; polars `describe` differs
and is not followed); `valueCounts` `normalize`/`sort`/`ascending`; `cut` `bins` count (the 0.1 % edge extension),
`precision`, `interval_labels` (pandas' interval text), `break_out` (polars `include_breaks`), `binEdges` and
`qcutEdges` (`retbins`); `rank` `pct`/`na_option`; `quantiles` (list of q, pandas `DataFrame.quantile([...])`) and
`Interpolation.equiprobable` (polars; pandas has none); `join` `indicator`, `validate` (`ValidationFailed`),
`left_suffix`, `sort`, `keep_right_keys` (polars `coalesce=False`), `on` defaulting to the common columns;
`SortKey.missing` (polars per-key `nulls_last`) and `sortByKey` (pandas `key=`; a cell callback, because
`mutate` + `sort` + `drop` already covers an `Expr` key, so `sort_by(expr)` needs no new verb); `fillna`
`per_column` and `limit`, `fillNull` `across_columns` (pandas `axis=1`); `pivot` `margins`/`margins_name`
(function over the rows, as pandas), `fill` of any kind, `sort_columns` (polars `false`), `pivotMany` `aggs` per value
(polars `separator` was already there); `interpolate` `limit`, `limit_direction`, `limit_area` (pandas) and the
methods `zero` and `slinear`; `ohlc`/`ohlcAggs` (groupby and, through `groupByDynamic`'s `aggs`, resample).
Engine notes: `zero` and `slinear` are not engine-checked (pandas needs SciPy, absent from the oracle venv); `slinear`
is the linear line between known points by `by`/position, `zero` the previous known value. `quantiles` of `lower`/
`higher`/`nearest` on an int column answers floats where pandas keeps ints. `describeWith` of a duration or
timestamp column is hand-tested only (the oracle cannot compare pandas' string form). Not done, with the reason:
polars `bin_intervals`/`bin_quantiles`/`bin_ranks` (their behaviour was not surveyed on a page; `cut`/`qcut` with
`break_out` serve the same uses), `pivotKeys` does not take the new `pivotMany` fields (use `pivotMany`), `validate`
of a `semi`/`anti`/`cross` join is not checked, `fillNull` `across_columns` for strategies other than
forward/backward, `interpolate` `limit*` counts rows in row order (an unsorted `by` is the caller's to sort).

`ranges.zig` (`intRange`, `intRanges`, `linearSpace`, `repeatValue`/`ones`/`zeros`, `dateRange`/`datetimeRange`

`is_between(closed)`, `concat_str(separator, ignore_nulls, na_rep)`, `fold` (the binary operators as data),
`business_day_count`, `make_date`/`make_datetime`/`make_duration`, `from_epoch`, and `RoundMode.toward_zero`
(`Expr.round` with that mode is the truncation at `decimals`; `Expr.truncate` was taken by the `dt` bucket
function); `Selector` gained `alpha`/`alphanumeric`/`digit` (by name; Unicode since wave W8) and `nested`; `names.zig`
(`renameWith`, `renameLower`/`renameUpper`, `renameReplace`); `colfn.zig` (`item`, `uniqueCounts`, `hist`,
`foldColumns`/`cumFoldColumns` with a callback, `cumSumHorizontal`, `alignFrames`). Engine answers:
`tools/oracle2b.py` to `src/oracle2b_vectors.json` (103 cases), replayed by `src/s2w3_oracle_test.zig`.
Differences kept: `cum_fold`/`cum_sum_horizontal` give one column per input where polars gives one struct column;
`hist` category text prints up to six decimals as polars does; `name.replace` replaces every match
(polars' regex form too, measured). **Left, with reasons:** `time_range`/`pl.time` (no time-of-day column
type); pandas' anchored frequencies other than months, weeks and business days (`BMS`, `W-MON`, ... are
named after calendars the duration language does not have; `1mo` from a month end and `business` cover
`ME`, `MS` and `B`); `cum_*(reverse=True)`, `diff(null_behavior)` and `over(order_by, mapping_strategy)` are wave W5's; (Unicode case in `renameLower`/`renameUpper` and the Unicode `alpha`/`alphanumeric`/`digit` came with wave W8); `cs.alpha(ignore_spaces=)`; `int_ranges` takes `?i64` slices, not columns of a frame.

**Wave W4 (dataframe S2, 2026-11-09): `str` and `dt` gaps, durations.** Built, each with the engine it follows (doc
comments say where the engines differ); engine answers in `tools/oracle2c.py` to `src/oracle2c_vectors.json` (293
cases, pandas 3.1 and polars 2.1), replayed by `src/s2w4_oracle_test.zig`; hand tests in `src/s2w4_test.zig`.
*Str* (`strfn.zig`, `Expr`): `split_ws` (Python `split()` / pandas default: runs of Unicode whitespace, no empty
pieces, `limit` pieces with the rest kept as is), `rsplit`, `partition`/`rpartition` (a record `{"0","1","2"}`, pandas'
column names), `split_fields` (polars `split_exact`: `n + 1` fields, the rest dropped; `rest`: `splitn`), `wrap`
(Python `textwrap.wrap`, joined by newlines, pandas `str.wrap`: `width`, `break_long_words`, `break_on_hyphens`;
`expand_tabs`, `replace_whitespace` and `drop_whitespace` at Python's defaults, the other options not offered; only the
space is whitespace after the replacement and bytes >= 0x80 count as letters for the hyphen rules), `slice_replace`,
`encode`/`decode` (`hex`, `base64`; decode gives text, null for invalid input or non-UTF-8 bytes: there is no binary
type, polars' `strict=True` raises where this nulls), `affix_any` (`startswith`/`endswith` with several affixes),
`replace_n` and `replace_regex.n` (pandas `n=`), `match_regex` (`match`, `fullmatch`: the whole pattern is anchored),
`Unary.is_ascii`; frame verbs `splitColumns` (pandas `split(expand=True)`, polars `split_exact` + `unnest`: literal,
regex or whitespace, `prefix`, as many columns as the widest cell, at most `max_str_columns`) and `strGetDummies`
(pandas `str.get_dummies(sep)`: int 0/1 columns by default, `as_bool` for `pd.get_dummies`'s bools; the token "" is a
column, as pandas). *Parsing without a format*: `Expr.to_datetime` with `DateMode.infer` (polars `str.strptime` with no
format, pandas default: the pattern is that of the column's first non-null cell, then applied to all; the expression
must be a column), `.iso8601` (pandas `format="ISO8601"`) and `.mixed` (each cell on its own), with `dayfirst`;
`dtfn.inferFormats` lists the patterns after ISO 8601 (`d/m/Y`, `d-m-Y`, `d.m.Y` and their month-first twins in the
order `dayfirst` sets, then `Y/m/d`, `Y.m.d` and English month names). Epoch numbers stay `from_epoch` (W3).
*Durations*: `DtPart.total_seconds_f64` (pandas' float; the `total_*` ints stay polars'), `td_days`, `td_seconds`
(0..86399, pandas' normalised field), `td_microseconds`, `td_nanoseconds` (always 0), `Expr.td_components` (a record,
pandas `components`); `aggregate` of a duration column gives a duration for `sum`/`mean`/`median`/`quantile`/`std`
(microseconds truncated toward zero) and of a timestamp column a timestamp for `mean`/`median`/`quantile` and a
duration for `std`; `readJson` `epoch_durations` (with `date_unit`, default `ms`, as pandas writes a `timedelta64`).
*dt*: `dt_combine` (a date plus a time of day given as microseconds or `HH:MM[:SS[.f]]` text, as `dt.time` writes it),
`dt_replace` (each part an `Expr`; **null on an invalid result where polars raises**), `tz_offset` (`base`, `dst`,
`total`; polars `base_utc_offset`/`dst_offset` and pandas `utcoffset`, over the sibling `tz`), `is_business_day` and
`add_business_days` with `week_mask`, `holidays` and `roll` (`forward`/`backward`; polars' default `raise` is not done).
**Differences kept:** pandas with `dayfirst=True` reads year-first text as year-day-month (`2024-01-05` is 1 May; its
own docs warn) and an inferred ISO column fixes the `T`/space separator from the first cell; neither is followed (ISO
8601 is read as ISO, cell by cell). Polars infers no month-name pattern (null); `infer` here knows pandas' names.
`total_seconds_f64` divides exactly where pandas multiplies by 1e-9 (relative difference 3e-11). The business-day
search gives null for a mask with no day on, a span past 2^30 days, or a holiday list that needs more than 4096
refinement steps. **Left, with reasons:** `str.cat` is `concat_str` (W3); pandas `str.extractall`/`partition` into a
DataFrame is the record plus `unnest`; Unicode case came with wave W8; `dt.combine` with a real `Time` (the
module has no time-of-day column); `components` as a frame verb (the record plus `unnest` is the same, and keeps
the verb count down); `time` strings other than `HH:MM[:SS[.f]]` in `combine`; the flags of `textwrap` not offered
(`initial_indent`, `subsequent_indent`, `max_lines`, `placeholder`, `fix_sentence_endings`, `tabsize`).
